newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German govt launches tax bill, talks in limbo.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German govt launches tax bill, talks in limbo.

text.p: The German government on Friday launched the first stage of major tax reforms in parliament as efforts to revive talks aimed at finding a compromise with the opposition degenerated into a slanging match.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel told parliament that early passage of his 1998 tax bill and planned legislation for 1999 would give "a decisive push for a positive turnaround in the German business climate".

As government tax reforms began their winding path through parliament, hopes of reaching a cross-party deal to prevent the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) blocking the reforms in the upper house of parliament received a serious blow.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine again demanded a personal meeting with Chancellor Helmut Kohl to restart the negotiations, which Lafontaine broke off in a recent row over government cuts in coal subsidies.
But he said Kohl must change tack on tax for the talks to make any sense. "We can't give a helping hand to policies which will make the rich even richer and the poor poorer," he said.
Lafontaine accused Kohl of financing German unification by forcing up the costs of employing labour instead of through taxation, with disastrous economic consequences.

He said occupational insurance costs had ballooned to 42 percent of wages from 34 percent before unification. "Cutting these costs is the most important task we face in Germany today," Lafontaine told party workers in Berlin.

Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) blamed the SPD for the failure to get talks going again. CDU general secretary Peter Hintze called Lafontaine's demand for a personal meeting with Kohl a "transparent diversionary manoeuvre".
"If the SPD continues to boycott the tax working group, it must take the full responsibility for the delay of tax reform," Hintze said.

Waigel's 1998 tax bill foresees cutting the main corporate and commercial income tax rates and unifying them at a common 40 percent rate. The cuts would be neutral for revenue as they would be offset by tightening up on corporate write-offs.

The bill would also cut two points off the solidarity surcharge on income tax, raised to aid eastern Germany, to 5.5 percent, lopping 7.5 billion marks ($4.4 billion) off the tax burden. The lion's share of a total 30 billion marks in income and corporate tax cuts would, however, come in 1999.

SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told parliament the coalition's tax measures would rip a huge hole in government finances and do nothing to cut unemployment, which is at a post-war record of 4.7 million.
The SPD says that if the reforms are implemented fully by 1999, Germany's budget deficit will badly overshoot targets required under European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The SPD figures, based on official projections, predict a surge in the deficit to 174 billion marks in 1999 -- equivalent to 4.4 percent of gross domestic product.
That would be up from an official target of 105 billion marks this year -- which just undercuts the Maastricht treaty's three percent limit.

Scharping added that renewed talks would only be possible if the coalition slashed labour costs this summer, cut taxes for ordinary workers from next year and put together solid counter-financing for the tax reforms.

"If you fulfil these conditions we will be ready to talk, because we will have to talk anyway," Scharping said, adding the two sides would be forced to seek a compromise eventually, if not in informal talks then in parliament.
